raw_response:
I am seventy years old, and to be honest I only started handling the farm myself last year. Before that, my son managed things, but he and his daughter-in-law went to work at a factory in Shijiazhuang, so now the land is on me and my wife. We have seven people under our roof, including three grandchildren in school, so there are many mouths to feed. My son sends some money home every month, but not much. Six mu of land — that is not a lot, but it is what we have.

Last year was my first full year doing everything myself. I mostly watched what Old Wang from the east end of the village did, and I asked my nephew — he has a bigger plot down by the canal and knows more than me. If they did something, I did the same. I do not read books and I do not go to those extension meetings; I cannot follow what they say anyway. I learn by watching and talking.

**Wheat — 3 mu**

It is October now, and everyone is planting winter wheat. I will get my seed in the ground right after the National Day holiday, around October 10th. I saved some seed from last year but not enough, so I will buy from the seed shop — whatever variety they have, probably that Jinmai type everyone plants. I hire the tractor guy to plow after the maize comes off, then I broadcast the seed and fertilizer by hand.

For fertilizer, Old Wang puts down one big bag of compound fertilizer per mu before planting — that is about 25 kg per mu, I think. Then in March when the wheat turns green, I topdress with urea, about half a bag, maybe 10 kg per mu. I know I should not put too much — fertilizer is expensive now, over 3 yuan per jin — but last year I probably used too little and the wheat looked yellow. This year I will do what Old Wang does: base plus one topdress. Two applications total.

Irrigation: I pump from the well. I will water before winter if the soil is dry, once at green-up in March, once at jointing, and maybe once when the grain is filling. Four times if I can afford it, but last year I only did three because the electricity bill was too high. Water costs 15–20 yuan each time now.

For pests, I will spray herbicide once in early spring when the weeds come up. I do not know the name — I just tell the shop "wheat herbicide" and they give me the bottle.

I will hire the combine for harvest in early June — 50 yuan per mu — because at my age I cannot swing a sickle fast enough. Last year my wheat got about 700 jin per mu, which is roughly 350 kg. It was less than Old Wang got, so this year I hope for about the same, maybe 400 kg if the spring rain is good.

**Summer maize — 3 mu (same fields after wheat)**

The window is very tight. Once the combine takes the wheat, I have only a few days. I hire the custom planter — he charges 30 yuan per mu — because I cannot plant fast enough myself at seventy. No time for real tillage; we just plant into the stubble.

I buy hybrid maize seed from the cooperative, about 40 yuan per mu. For fertilizer, one application at planting: about 20 kg of compound fertilizer per mu. If the leaves look yellow when the plants are knee-high, I might side-dress a little urea, but last year I did not bother and it was fine. So maybe one application, maybe two.

Irrigate once or twice, depending on the summer rains. If July is wet, maybe only once in August.

Labor is mostly family — my wife and I thin the seedlings and weed by hand. My grandson helps on weekends. I might hire no one for maize except the planter.

Last year I got about 450 kg per mu. I will hope for 450 kg again.

**Cotton — 2 mu**

I just finished picking the last bolls this week. It is hard work for old hands — bending over all day — but cotton brings cash, which we need. I will plant again in late April.

I buy hybrid cotton seed, about 50 yuan per mu. Fertilizer: less than wheat. One bag of compound fertilizer per mu at planting, about 20 kg, and then a little urea when it flowers. Maybe 10 kg of nitrogen total per mu. Irrigate twice — once in June and once in July if it is dry.

Pesticide is important for cotton — bollworms always come. I spray insecticide twice and use herbicide once. The shopkeeper tells me which one; I do not remember the names.

Picking is the problem. My wife and I can only do so much. Last year we fell behind and some bolls opened late. This year I will hire two women from the village to help pick, paying them by the jin. That is cash out of pocket, so if money is tight I might skip it and just pick slower.

Last year my cotton yield was not great — about 300 jin of seed cotton per mu, which I think is roughly 160 kg of lint after ginning. I will hope for 180 kg per mu this year if the bollworms do not get bad.

**Stevia — 1 mu**

My nephew talked me into this last year. He said the sweet-leaf buyers pay good money. I do not really understand this crop — I just do what my nephew tells me. I plant in mid-April, around the same time as cotton.

I put down less fertilizer than the other crops — about 15 kg of compound fertilizer per mu, one application before planting. That is maybe 8 kg of nitrogen. I water it when it looks dry, probably twice this year. If bugs come, I will ask my nephew what to spray.

My wife and I weed it by hand with hoes. No hired labor — the plot is too small.

Last year I got about 150 kg of dried leaves per mu. I hope for 180 kg this year, but honestly I do not know what I am doing with this crop.

**Money and labor**

I have about 3,000 yuan saved for inputs this year. Fertilizer prices worry me — they went up again. If I run short, I will cut back on the stevia or cotton first, and make sure the wheat gets fed. Wheat is the safest. We need the grain to eat and to sell.

For labor, my wife and I do most of the work. My son comes home for wheat harvest and maybe a few days in summer, but he cannot lose factory wages. My grandchildren help on weekends but they have school. Hired labor is only for the combine, the maize planter, and maybe cotton picking. We have to be careful with cash.

I am not trying to get rich. At my age, with only one year of experience, I just want to keep everyone fed, pay for the grandchildren's school supplies, and have a little cash left for medicine. I follow what my neighbors do, I do not take big risks, and I pray the weather is better than last year.
